answer.evidence: The building is a flat, face-on facade of stacked vertical bands: upper floor, windows, ledge, signboard and shutter. The silhouette is a constant 98px wide from row 14 to row 143, with a 2px jog at rows 79-82. No roof, awning or tile slope is drawn. The topmost rows 14-16 are only a pale 2-row rim plus a 1-row dark outline at the edge, not a horizontal surface. The ledge at rows 79-82 is a front-facing strip with no edge line or eave shadow. The row 28-50 area at the top only shows plants as decor and windows, which are vertical faces. No part of the main body shows a top surface.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a modern shuttered shop front, and the references are tiled-roof houses. Both are whole buildings, so the kind matches. Measured facts: 8 visible tones per tile vs 12 and 10 in the references, and 19% near-flat coverage vs 0% in both references. The blue sign band and the grey wall bands are large flat areas with only 2-3 steps. The shutter has slat lines, but little per-slat highlight or grain. The outline is a dark grey-blue tint, not neutral (0% neutral edge pixels), so it is not a sticker-look black line. It is still a uniform frame around each panel rather than a selective material-toned edge. The upper panel has some detail (plants, AC unit, window glass reflections), but the overall shading is shallower and flatter than the Beodeul references, with no scalloped tiles, plaster speckle or stone shading. Because the flat fills are measurable and the shading is shallow, it falls short of the references.
